children.text: With the NAFTA House vote set for November 17th, the Clinton administration intensified efforts to win over undecided members, including several in the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, with negotiations over a proposed North American Development Bank for border and environmental cleanup as a key sticking point. Operation Blockade in El Paso was officially renamed a permanent enhanced patrol initiative, with Border Patrol spokesperson Doug Moser saying arrest numbers were up 80 percent and there were no plans for a moratorium despite calls from Catholic bishops in the region to pause the operation. Health officials at a Los Angeles hearing reported that Latino/as constituted the fastest-growing segment of new AIDS cases, with a 95 percent increase in HIV infection among Hispanic men in the past year alone. And the Congressional Hispanic Caucus lost a floor fight over a bill extending unemployment benefits that was funded partly by requiring legal immigrants to wait five years rather than three to qualify for government aid, with Congressman Luis Gutierrez arguing that immigrants were being scapegoated for economic problems they had nothing to do with.

Arturo Rodriguez, named to lead the United Farm Workers following Cesar Chavez's death the previous April, was in Washington to address the American Federation of Teachers. He described efforts to sustain the grape boycott, expand pesticide awareness campaigns, and train new union staff. Rodriguez also said the UFW had not yet made any payment on a $ 2.9 million judgment stemming from a lawsuit against the Bruce Church Lettuce Company, and was appealing the decision, given that Chavez had died while testifying in that very case. Rodriguez noted a renewed national interest in farm worker issues in the months since Chavez's death.

Filmmaker Hector Galan joined Maria Hinojosa to discuss his documentary for the American Experience series on PBS. Galan described the challenge of depicting Villa as a complex historical figure rather than a caricature, drawing on interviews with witnesses to the 1916 Columbus, New Mexico raid and on filming done in Chihuahua. He said Americans who were attacked by Villa's forces saw only a violent outlaw, while poor Mexicans viewed him as a champion of the dispossessed. Galan, who is Chicano, acknowledged the tension of approaching Villa as both a cultural icon and an at times brutal historical figure.

Two hundred social workers gathered in Denver to form HART, Hispanic Addictions Resources and Training, a nationwide network dedicated to addressing alcohol and drug abuse in Latino/a communities. Organizers pointed to a shortage of Latino/a professionals in social work, a lack of research data on Hispanic addiction patterns, and the need for culturally specific treatment approaches that account for the diversity within Latino/a communities.
Guillermo Gomez-Peña: Accused of Kidnapping His Own Son

Performance artist and commentator Guillermo Gomez-Peña described being stopped by police in the San Diego area after two women at a restaurant called 911 to report that a brown-skinned Latino man with a ponytail appeared to be holding a blonde Anglo boy against his will. The child was Gomez-Peña's own four-year-old son. He and his son were detained for 45 minutes before he could produce press credentials. Gomez-Peña reflected that the incident was not exceptional but representative of the racial paranoia and civilian vigilantism faced daily by Latinos across the country. He noted that in the aftermath, his son began leaving his father's last name off his school drawings.
